clue.text: Alan Ayckbourn taking a leaf from Ben Travers's book?

definitions.text: Alan Ayckbourn taking a leaf from Ben Travers's book?

parts.words: Alan Ayckbourn taking a leaf from Ben Travers's book?
parts.note: Ben Travers wrote the Aldwych farces, so Ayckbourn borrowing his manner points to an Ayckbourn comedy of the same genre set among beds

explanation.surface: A modern playwright is accused of copying an older master of stage comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Travers was the British writer of the 1920s Aldwych farces; Ayckbourn's 1975 play of this title is a farce played out across three couples' sleeping quarters.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of an Ayckbourn comedy, a farce set in the sleeping quarters of three couples.

clue.text: Highly spoken-of dramatist from "magnificence" to "the genius "

definitions.text: Highly spoken-of dramatist from "magnificence" to "the genius "

parts.words: Highly spoken-of dramatist from "magnificence" to "the genius "
parts.note: Magnificence (1973) and The Genius (1983) are plays by the same British political playwright, Howard

explanation.surface: A celebrated playwright's career is traced from one acclaimed work to another.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted words are titles: Howard Brenton wrote Magnificence and The Genius, so the clue spans his career.
explanation.definitionFit: Howard Brenton is the British playwright who wrote both Magnificence and The Genius.

clue.text: Australian yarn-spinner from Hardy's only essay on the subject

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow, running across the join

explanation.surface: Thomas Hardy is said to have written only a single essay on some topic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' takes the run across 'HarDY'S ONly'. Edward Dyson was an Australian short-story writer and balladeer.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Dyson was an Australian writer of tales and bush stories, a teller of yarns.

clue.text: That's us, in Pope-inspired title from O'Hara

explanation.surface: A title by O'Hara borrows from Alexander Pope and refers to the speaker and companions.
explanation.walkthrough: John O'Hara's novel Ourselves to Know takes its title from Pope's Essay on Man: 'And all our knowledge is, ourselves to know'.
explanation.definitionFit: The first is the reflexive pronoun for 'we'; the second is the opening word of O'Hara's novel title taken from Pope.

clue.text: But did thee feel the earth (? Ernest Hemingway)

definitions.text: But did thee feel the earth (? Ernest Hemingway)

parts.words: But did thee feel the earth (? Ernest Hemingway)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the famous line from For Whom the Bell Tolls needs its missing final verb

explanation.surface: A lover's question from a Hemingway novel, with its last word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: In For Whom the Bell Tolls, Pilar asks Maria and Robert whether the ground shifted beneath them; the clue omits the verb at the end of that line.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb of the quotation, meaning shift position or stir.

clue.text: Curiously smart air of Golden Temple city

indicators.note: curiously signals the letters of the next words come out in an odd, unexpected order

explanation.surface: A visitor notices a strange, smart air about the city of the Golden Temple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curiously' rearranges SMART AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: The Golden Temple, holiest shrine of Sikhism, stands in this Punjab city.

clue.text: The modest construction of Blasco Ibáñez

explanation.surface: A Spanish novelist's humble building is described.
explanation.walkthrough: Blasco Ibáñez's novel La barraca appeared in English as The Cabin.
explanation.definitionFit: A small simple hut is a modest construction, and it names the English title of Blasco Ibáñez's novel La barraca.

clue.text: Lionel, a crime-writer heard during Frost report?

explanation.surface: A crime novelist is mentioned while a satirical TV programme is broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: The Frost Report was David Frost's 1960s BBC show; while it ran, the announcement 'David's on' sounds just like the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Lionel Davidson wrote thrillers; spoken quickly, 'David's on' names the presenter Frost being on air.

clue.text: Characters in ID room might pin down similar looking twin

indicators.note: characters means letters, so the letters in the next words are to be used in a new order

explanation.surface: Identifying one of two lookalikes in an identity parade room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters in' takes the letters of ID ROOM to rearrange. The Comedy of Errors has two twin servants of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors the twin servants share one name and identical looks.

clue.text: A flower of New York from Sholem Asch

explanation.surface: A bloom of Manhattan is attributed to a Yiddish novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is the crossword's thing that flows, a river. Sholem Asch wrote the novel East River.
explanation.definitionFit: A tidal strait running past Manhattan, and the title of a Sholem Asch novel.

clue.text: Orwell for prime minister?

explanation.surface: George Orwell is suggested as a candidate for Downing Street.
explanation.walkthrough: Orwell's real name was Eric Blair; Tony Blair was UK Prime Minister 1997-2007.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric was George Orwell's real surname, and Tony was the Labour Prime Minister of that name.

clue.text: Paul Bowles's white knight makes points in curiously true setting

indicators.note: in here sits the two compass letters inside the rearranged word
curiously tells us the word true appears in an unexpected order

parts.note: points of the compass, north and north, each abbreviated N

explanation.surface: A chivalrous character from Bowles makes his case in a strangely truthful setting.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass 'points' here are two norths. Tunner is the American friend in Bowles's The Sheltering Sky who gallantly tries to rescue Kit, hence 'white knight'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunner, in The Sheltering Sky, is the chivalrous friend who tries to rescue Kit.

clue.text: Strange sun midst evangelical sect

indicators.note: strange signals that the letters of the next words are put in an odd new order

explanation.surface: Something odd lies in the middle of the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges SUN MIDST. The Stundists were a 19th-century Ukrainian Protestant movement.
explanation.definitionFit: Stundism was a Protestant revivalist movement among Ukrainian peasants, named after the German 'Stunde' for its Bible hours.

clue.text: Indigenous, like Morley Callaghan's argosy

explanation.surface: Something home-grown is likened to a Canadian novelist's fleet.
explanation.walkthrough: Morley Callaghan's first story collection was A Native Argosy (1929).
explanation.definitionFit: Native means born in a place; it is also the first word of Callaghan's book title.

clue.text: Hughes poem harder to handle than Lawrence's "Nettles "?

definitions.text: Hughes poem harder to handle than Lawrence's "Nettles "?

parts.words: Hughes poem harder to handle than Lawrence's "Nettles "?
parts.note: D. H. Lawrence wrote a collection called Nettles; Ted Hughes wrote a poem named after an even pricklier plant

explanation.surface: Comparing two poets' prickly plant poems for how painful they are to grasp.
explanation.walkthrough: Lawrence's late verse collection was Nettles; Ted Hughes's poem is about spiky Scottish-emblem weeds, pricklier to grip than stinging plants.
explanation.definitionFit: Ted Hughes's poem on spiny weeds that are worse to grasp than stinging nettles.

clue.text: Appeal is to nymph who found favour with Zeus

definitions.text: nymph who found favour with Zeus

parts.note: an appeal is a call, as in a call for help

explanation.surface: Someone appeals to a nymph who caught the eye of the king of the gods.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this nymph was loved by Zeus and turned into a bear, then the Great Bear constellation.

clue.text: "A little mild expostulation or —" (Tom Brown at Oxford)

definitions.text: "A little mild expostulation or —" (Tom Brown at Oxford)

parts.words: "A little mild expostulation or —" (Tom Brown at Oxford)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Thomas Hughes's sequel novel: the gap is a word for scolding someone at length

explanation.surface: A line from a Victorian college novel with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Brown at Oxford is Thomas Hughes's sequel to Tom Brown's School Days; the blank pairs with 'mild expostulation' as another word for a reproving talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Delivering a reproving talk, a stronger partner to mild expostulation.

clue.text: Olivier portrayed his father, while Marlowe's was the younger

explanation.surface: An actor played a writer's parent, while a Tudor playwright's character was the junior one.
explanation.walkthrough: Olivier played John Mortimer's father in A Voyage Round My Father; in Marlowe's Edward II, Mortimer Junior is the king's enemy.
explanation.definitionFit: Olivier played the father of playwright John Mortimer; Marlowe's Edward II has Mortimer the younger as the queen's lover.

clue.text: Bobby's chambermaid suggests loose sandal

explanation.surface: A servant's name brings to mind a floppy piece of footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: In Fielding's Joseph Andrews, Mrs Slipslop is the waiting-woman to Lady Booby; the word also means a loose slipper.
explanation.definitionFit: Fielding named Lady Booby's maid Mrs Slipslop, and the word also means a slack, shuffling slipper.

clue.text: A learner in some Wilde leading role

indicators.note: in places the article and learner letter within the word some

parts.note: L is the learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A novice actor takes on a starring part in an Oscar Wilde play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts A and L inside SOME. Salome is Wilde's one-act tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Wilde's play is its central part, the princess who dances for Herod.

clue.text: Twice in charge, holding negative return for sort of conventional Greek sculpture

indicators.note: holding says the doubled letters wrap around the turned word
twice says the abbreviation for in charge is written two times over
return here means the word for negative is read backwards

explanation.surface: A leader with double authority rejects a style of Greek statue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice in charge' doubles the IC abbreviation. Iconic statues of Greek victors were made to a fixed conventional pattern rather than as portraits.
explanation.definitionFit: Iconic statues of Greek athletes followed a fixed conventional type, so the adjective names that style.

clue.text: Remains when actor laughs inopportunely

explanation.surface: A performer breaks up at the wrong moment, as dead bodies are discussed.
explanation.walkthrough: In theatre slang an actor who corpses gets the giggles on stage, ruining a scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Dead bodies are remains, and in stage jargon to corpse is to break into untimely laughter.

clue.text: Some polite, rational, scholarly folk

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Describing some people as courteous, sensible and learned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes the run from 'poLITE, RATIonal'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means educated people interested in books and learning.

clue.text: Drinking companion of Gloucester poet

parts.note: Laurie Lee's Gloucestershire memoir is titled Cider with a girl's name; that girl shared the drink

explanation.surface: Asking who drank alongside a West Country poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurie Lee's memoir Cider with Rosie tells of his Gloucestershire childhood; the girl in the title shared the cider.
explanation.definitionFit: The girl in Laurie Lee's title Cider with Rosie, with whom he drank cider.

clue.text: Note, not necessarily tremolo

explanation.surface: A musical note is said not to be a tremolo in every case.
explanation.walkthrough: A tremolo is a rapid repetition or wavering in music; to tremble in the voice may be a tremolo but need not be.
explanation.definitionFit: An eighth note in music, and a trembling or wavering of the voice that need not be a formal tremolo.

clue.text: Composer showing ill-directed drive

indicators.note: ill-directed suggests the word drive is sent the wrong way, its letters disordered

explanation.surface: A composer is shown to have poorly focused ambition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ill-directed' rearranges DRIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Verdi was the Italian composer of Aida and La traviata.

clue.text: Coy comment

parts.note: a remark made with knowing, playful slyness is described with a word for teasingly mischievous

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes a remark that is playfully sly, a knowing kind of coyness.

clue.text: Encounters in first part of Sassoon's autobiographical novel

definitions.text: first part of Sassoon's autobiographical novel

explanation.surface: Encounters happen in the opening section of a war poet's fictional memoir.
explanation.walkthrough: Sassoon's Memoirs of a Fox-Hunting Man is the first part of his fictionalised autobiography; hunt gatherings are called this.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means comes across someone; it is also the noun for fox-hunting gatherings that open Sassoon's memoir.

clue.text: Drastically rig dramas for pre-Lenten festival

indicators.note: drastically signals the letters of the next words are radically rearranged

explanation.surface: Theatre plays are fixed in extreme fashion ahead of Lent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drastically' rearranges RIG DRAMAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrove Tuesday, the carnival day of feasting before Lent begins, French for 'fat Tuesday'.

clue.text: Shavian phoneticist

parts.note: the professor of speech in Bernard Shaw's Pygmalion who teaches Eliza Doolittle

explanation.definitionFit: The professor of speech sounds in Shaw's Pygmalion who transforms Eliza Doolittle.
